learner:
Level: beginner theory, intermediate ear player; knows open chords and some barre chords, cannot read notation.
Goal: understand keys and chords well enough to write original chord progressions.
Known: can name the notes of the C major scale; correctly guessed that a key has seven chords.
Gap: does not know what makes a chord minor (the third), so chord quality, key chords and function must be built from intervals up.

lessons.title: Half Steps and Whole Steps on the Fretboard
lessons.objective: Measure distances between notes in half steps and whole steps using frets.
lessons.hook: Every scale and chord is built from these two step sizes, so they are the ruler for everything that follows.
lessons.aside: Sharps and flats are two names for the same black-key note, so A# and Bb sound identical.
lessons.explain: There are 12 different notes before the pattern repeats an octave higher. A half step is the distance of one fret on the guitar. A whole step equals two half steps, or two frets. Letter names hide the sharps: A to B is a whole step because A# sits between them. E to F and B to C are half steps; all other neighboring letter notes are whole steps apart. Example: on the low E string, open is E and fret 1 is F, a half step. Fret 3 is G, a whole step above F.
key_facts: A half step is the distance of one fret on the guitar.
A whole step equals two half steps, or two frets.
There are 12 different notes before the pattern repeats an octave higher.
E to F and B to C are half steps; all other neighboring letter notes are whole steps apart.

predict.q: On the B string, how many frets up from the open B is the note C?

angles: Picture a piano. Every key, black or white, is one half step from the next key. Find the places where two white keys touch with no black key between them, then work out which letter names those are.

Treat the frets like rungs on a ladder. Each rung is the smallest possible step, and skipping one rung covers two of those steps. Try climbing the G string from the open G and name each note you land on.
claims: A half step is one fret on a guitar.
A whole step is two half steps.
There are 12 distinct pitch names per octave in Western music.
E–F and B–C are half steps; other adjacent natural notes are whole steps.

items.q: On a single string, how far is a half step?
items.why: A half step is the smallest move on the guitar, which is one fret.
misconceptions: A half step is the same size as a whole step
A half step is the size of a minor third
A half step spans a whole octave

items.q: Which pair of letter notes is only a half step apart?
items.why: B–C has no sharp between the two notes, so it is a half step.
misconceptions: Every pair of neighboring letters is a half step
Every pair of neighboring letters is a half step
Every pair of neighboring letters is a half step

items.q: You are on fret 5 of the A string, which is the note D. A whole step up lands on which fret?
items.why: A whole step is two frets, so 5 + 2 = 7.
misconceptions: A whole step is one fret
A whole step is three frets
A whole step means doubling the fret number

items.q: How many different notes are there before the pattern repeats at the octave?
items.why: There are 7 letter names plus 5 sharps or flats, which makes 12 notes.
misconceptions: Only the letter names count as notes
The repeated octave note counts as a new note
Sharps and flats are counted only some of the time

items.q: What note is a whole step above E?
items.why: E to F is only a half step, so you need one more half step to reach F#.

items.q: If you move from fret 4 to fret 5 on one string, what distance have you moved?
items.why: One fret equals one half step.

lessons.title: The Major Scale Step Pattern
lessons.objective: Build a major scale on any starting note using the whole and half step pattern.
lessons.hook: The major scale is the toolbox that a key's chords come from.
lessons.explain: The major scale follows the step pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half, so half steps fall between degrees 3–4 and 7–8. A major scale has seven different notes, then repeats at the octave. The C major scale uses only natural notes because its half steps land on E–F and B–C. On any other starting note, the pattern needs sharps or flats to keep the steps right. Starting the pattern on G requires F# instead of F. Example: G A B C D E F# G. E to F# is the whole step the pattern needs, and F# to G is the final half step.
key_facts: The major scale follows the step pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half, so half steps fall between degrees 3–4 and 7–8.
A major scale has seven different notes, then repeats at the octave.
Starting the pattern on G requires F# instead of F.
The C major scale uses only natural notes because its half steps land on E–F and B–C.

predict.q: If you play C major's notes but start and end on G, which note sounds wrong near the top?

angles: Picture the pattern as a fence with gaps: two long gaps, one short gap, three long gaps, then one short gap. Lay that fence on the A string starting from the open string and note which frets you hit.
Sing do-re-mi-fa-sol-la-ti-do slowly. Two of the moves feel squeezed compared with the others. Find which syllables they sit between, then count those positions.

rungs.text: Build D major: start on D. Whole step → E. Whole → F#. Half → G. Whole → A. Whole → B. Whole → C#. Half → D. Result: D E F# G A B C# D.
Build A major: start on A. Whole → B. Whole → __. Half → D. Whole → E. Whole → __. Whole → __. Half → A.
Build F major using the pattern. One note will need a flat.

claims: The major scale pattern is W W H W W W H.
Half steps in a major scale fall between degrees 3–4 and 7–8.
A major scale has seven distinct notes.
G major contains F#.
C major has no sharps or flats.

items.q: Which step pattern builds a major scale?
options: W W H W W W H
W H W W H W W
W W W H W W H
H W W W H W W
items.answer: W W H W W W H
items.why: This is the major scale pattern, with half steps after the 3rd and 7th notes.
misconceptions: This is the natural minor pattern
The first half step comes after the third whole step
The scale starts with a half step

items.q: Which note is in G major but not in C major?
items.why: Built on G, the pattern requires F# as the 7th note.
misconceptions: G major has the same sharp as D major
G major uses flats
The root's neighbor is always sharpened

items.q: How many different notes are in a major scale?
items.why: There are seven notes, and the eighth is the root repeated at the octave.
misconceptions: The repeated octave counts as a new note
A major scale is the same as a pentatonic scale
A major scale uses all 12 notes

items.q: Why does C major need no sharps or flats?
options: Its half steps fall on E–F and B–C naturally
C is the lowest note in all music
Major scales never use any sharps
Guitars are tuned with C as the root
items.answer: Its half steps fall on E–F and B–C naturally
items.why: The pattern's half steps match the natural half steps E–F and B–C.
misconceptions: C has a special place as the start of music
Major scales are always built from natural notes only
Guitar tuning decides a scale's notes

items.q: Between which scale degrees do the half steps fall in a major scale?
accept: third and fourth, seventh and eighth
items.why: The pattern W W H W W W H puts half steps after the 3rd and 7th notes.

items.q: Spell the G major scale.
items.answer: G A B C D E F# G
accept: G A B C D E F#
G, A, B, C, D, E, F sharp
items.why: Applying W W H W W W H from G requires F#.

lessons.title: Intervals: Thirds and Fifths
lessons.objective: Identify major thirds, minor thirds and perfect fifths by counting half steps.
lessons.hook: Chords are stacks of thirds, so telling a 3-fret gap from a 4-fret gap is the whole secret of chord quality.
lessons.explain: An interval is the distance between two notes, counted in half steps. A major third spans 4 half steps. A minor third spans 3 half steps. Both skip one letter name, so only the half step count tells them apart. A perfect fifth spans 7 half steps. Example: C to E is 4 half steps, a major third. E to G is 3 half steps, a minor third. C to G is 7 half steps, a perfect fifth. On one string, count the frets between the two notes.
key_facts: An interval is the distance between two notes, counted in half steps.
A major third spans 4 half steps.
A minor third spans 3 half steps.
A perfect fifth spans 7 half steps.
angles: Measure on one string by counting frets from the first note to the second. Try the open low E up to the G at fret 3, then decide which kind of interval that count represents.
A third always skips one letter, as in C to E skipping D. The letter skip looks the same for both kinds of third, so count frets to see which kind you have.
claims: An interval is measured in half steps.
A major third is 4 half steps.
A minor third is 3 half steps.
A perfect fifth is 7 half steps.

items.q: How many half steps are in a major third?
items.why: A major third spans 4 half steps.
misconceptions: Major and minor thirds are swapped
A major third is the same as a fourth
A third is the same as a fifth

items.q: D up to F is which interval?
items.why: D to F is 3 half steps (D–D#–E–F), which is a minor third.
misconceptions: Every third that skips one letter is major
A third and a fifth are the same thing
Notes one letter apart are a whole step even when a letter is skipped

items.q: C up to G spans how many half steps?
items.why: C to G is a perfect fifth, which spans 7 half steps.
misconceptions: Letter distance equals the number of half steps
A perfect fifth is an extra half step wide
A perfect fifth is 6 half steps

items.q: How is an interval measured?
options: How loud two notes sound together
items.why: An interval is the pitch distance between two notes, counted in half steps.
misconceptions: Interval size depends on guitar strings
An interval describes volume
An interval describes rhythm

items.q: What note is a major third above G?
items.why: Counting 4 half steps from G gives G#, A, A#, B.

items.q: What note is a minor third above A?
items.why: Counting 3 half steps from A gives A#, B, C.

lessons.title: What Makes a Chord Major or Minor
lessons.objective: Spell major and minor triads and explain that the third decides the chord's quality.
lessons.hook: You will finally know why E and Em sound happy and sad when only one note changes.
lessons.explain: A triad is three notes: a root, a third, and a fifth. A major triad is a major third plus a minor third, with a perfect fifth from root to top. Example: C–E–G. A minor triad has a minor third above the root, with the same perfect fifth. Example: C–Eb–G. The only difference between a major and a minor chord is the third, lowered by one half step in minor. On guitar, open E major has G# on the G string. Lift that finger and the open G string sounds instead, which gives E minor.
key_facts: A triad is three notes: a root, a third, and a fifth.
A major triad is a major third plus a minor third, with a perfect fifth from root to top.
A minor triad has a minor third above the root, with the same perfect fifth.
The only difference between a major and a minor chord is the third, lowered by one half step in minor.
fixes: Did not know what makes a chord minor

predict.q: Play open E major, then lift the finger off the G string. What happens?
options: It becomes an E power chord

angles: Think of a chord as a sandwich. The bread on the top and bottom stays put, and the filling sets the flavor. Play open G major and work out which of its notes is the filling you would move to change the mood.
Count half steps. In C major, count from C up to E and from E up to G. Then do the same for C, Eb, G. Notice which two counts swapped places.
claims: A triad has a root, third and fifth.
A major triad is a major third with a minor third on top.
A minor triad has a minor third above the root.
Both major and minor triads have a perfect fifth.
Lowering the third by a half step turns a major chord into a minor chord.
Open E major contains G# on the G string; E minor uses open G.

items.q: What turns A major into A minor?
options: Lowering the third a half step
Lowering the fifth a half step
Raising the root a half step
items.answer: Lowering the third a half step
items.why: Major and minor chords differ only in the third.
misconceptions: The fifth decides whether a chord is major or minor
Changing the root changes the quality
Minor chords are major chords with extra notes added

items.q: Which notes spell D minor?
items.why: D to F is a minor third and D to A is a perfect fifth.
misconceptions: D major is a minor chord
A minor chord's fifth is lowered as well
A minor chord replaces its third with a second

items.q: What are the three notes of a triad called?
items.why: A triad stacks a third and a fifth above the root.
misconceptions: Triads are built from seconds
Triads use a fourth instead of a third
Triads use three neighboring notes

items.q: In a C major chord, what interval is E up to G?
items.why: A major triad is a major third (C–E) with a minor third (E–G) on top.
misconceptions: A major chord is built from two major thirds
The top two notes of a chord form the fifth
Neighboring chord tones are one fret apart

items.q: You play open E major. Which single note changes to make E minor, and what does it become?
accept: the G# on the G string becomes open G
items.why: G# is the third of E major, and lowering it a half step gives the minor third G.

items.q: How many half steps are there from the root to the third in a minor chord?
items.why: A minor chord has a minor third above the root, which is 3 half steps.

lessons.title: The Diminished Triad
lessons.objective: Spell a diminished triad and recognize the ° symbol.
lessons.hook: Every major key contains one diminished chord, and you need to recognize it to complete the set.
lessons.explain: A diminished triad stacks two minor thirds. The diminished triad's fifth is 6 half steps above the root, one half step smaller than a perfect fifth. That shrunken fifth gives the chord its tense, unstable sound. B diminished is spelled B–D–F. B to D is 3 half steps and D to F is 3 half steps, so B to F is 6. Diminished chords are written with a ° symbol, as in B°. Compare B minor (B–D–F#): it has the same third, but its fifth is a half step higher.
key_facts: A diminished triad stacks two minor thirds.
The diminished triad's fifth is 6 half steps above the root, one half step smaller than a perfect fifth.
B diminished is spelled B–D–F.
Diminished chords are written with a ° symbol, as in B°.
angles: Start from a minor chord you know, such as Am (A–C–E). Ask what happens to its sound and spelling if the top note slides down one fret.
On one string, take a three-fret jump from G, then another three-fret jump from where you land. Name all three notes and count the total frets.
claims: A diminished triad consists of two stacked minor thirds.
A diminished fifth is 6 half steps.
B diminished is B–D–F.
The ° symbol marks a diminished chord.

items.q: What is a diminished triad built from?
options: A major then a minor third
A minor then a major third
items.why: A diminished triad stacks two minor thirds.
misconceptions: This describes an augmented chord
This describes a major chord
This describes a minor chord

items.q: Which notes spell B diminished?
items.why: B–D and D–F are both minor thirds.
misconceptions: B major is diminished
B minor is diminished
Diminished chords use a second instead of a third

items.q: How many half steps are there from the root to the fifth in a diminished triad?
items.why: The diminished fifth is one half step smaller than the perfect fifth's 7.
misconceptions: A diminished chord keeps the perfect fifth
The fifth is enlarged rather than shrunk
The fifth is lowered by a whole step

items.q: What does C#° mean?
options: C sharp played an octave up
items.why: The ° symbol marks a diminished chord.
misconceptions: ° means a seventh chord
° means a power chord
° marks an octave

items.q: How does a diminished triad's fifth differ from a minor triad's fifth?
items.answer: It is one half step lower: 6 half steps instead of 7.
items.why: Minor triads have a perfect fifth, while diminished triads shrink it by a half step.

items.q: Spell E diminished.
items.why: Stacking two minor thirds from E gives G, then Bb.

lessons.title: The Seven Chords of a Major Key
lessons.objective: Build all seven chords of a major key by stacking scale notes, and name each chord's quality.
lessons.hook: These seven chords are the palette you will write every progression from.
lessons.explain: Diatonic chords are built by stacking every other note of the scale on each scale degree. Using only scale notes, the size of each third decides the chord's quality. A major key has seven diatonic triads, one on each scale degree. In C major the chords are C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am, B°. Example: on D, take D, skip E, take F, skip G, take A. D–F is a minor third, so the chord is Dm. In every major key the qualities follow major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished.
key_facts: Diatonic chords are built by stacking every other note of the scale on each scale degree.
A major key has seven diatonic triads, one on each scale degree.
In C major the chords are C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am, B°.
In every major key the qualities follow major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished.

predict.q: Using only C major's notes, what chord do you get when you stack thirds on G?

angles: Write C D E F G A B twice in a row. Starting from any letter, circle every other letter until you have three, then count half steps to judge that chord's quality.
On guitar, play C major scale notes on the top strings and move one three-note shape up one scale step at a time. Listen for which chords sound bright and which sound dark.

rungs.text: Chord on D in C major: take D, skip E, take F, skip G, take A → D–F–A. D to F is 3 half steps, so the chord is Dm.
Chord on E in C major: take E, skip F, take __, skip A, take __ → E–G–B. E to G is __ half steps, so the chord is __.
Build the chord on A in C major and name its quality.

claims: Diatonic triads are built by stacking alternate scale notes.
A major key has seven diatonic triads.
C major's triads are C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am, B°.
Major-key triad qualities run major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished.

items.q: Which chord is NOT in C major?
items.why: D major needs F#, but C major's chord on D is Dm.
misconceptions: The vi chord is major
The IV chord is minor
The iii chord is major

items.q: In any major key, what is the quality of the chord on the 6th degree?
items.why: The quality pattern puts minor on the 6th degree.
misconceptions: Chords on higher degrees are major
The diminished chord sits on the 6th degree
Major keys contain augmented chords

items.q: How many diatonic triads are in a major key?
items.why: There is one triad on each of the seven scale degrees.
misconceptions: The diminished chord doesn't count
The octave gets its own chord
Every chromatic note gets a chord

items.q: Which notes make the diatonic triad on F in C major?
items.why: Stacking every other scale note from F gives F, A, C.
misconceptions: Chords are built from neighboring scale notes
Notes from outside the scale can be used
Every triad on F is minor

items.q: List the seven chords of C major.
items.answer: C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am, B°
accept: C Dm Em F G Am Bdim
C, D minor, E minor, F, G, A minor, B diminished
items.why: Stacking thirds within C major gives these chords.

items.q: Which scale degree of a major key holds the diminished chord?
items.why: The quality pattern ends with diminished on the 7th degree.

lessons.title: Roman Numeral Chord Names
lessons.objective: Name a key's chords with Roman numerals and convert numerals to chord names in C.
lessons.hook: Numerals let you describe a progression once and play it in any key.
lessons.explain: Roman numerals name chords by scale degree, so the same numbers work in any key. Uppercase numerals mean major chords and lowercase numerals mean minor chords. The diminished chord is lowercase with a °. The major-key numerals are I, ii, iii, IV, V, vi, vii°. In C major, IV is F, V is G, and vi is Am. Example: a song that goes I–IV–V uses C–F–G in C.
key_facts: Roman numerals name chords by scale degree, so the same numbers work in any key.
Uppercase numerals mean major chords and lowercase numerals mean minor chords.
The major-key numerals are I, ii, iii, IV, V, vi, vii°.
In C major, IV is F, V is G, and vi is Am.
angles: Think of house numbers. Saying 'the third house on the street' works on any street, even though the street name changes. Try numbering the chords of a song you already play.
The size of the numeral carries the mood: a big numeral is a bright chord and a small one is darker. Check this idea against vii° in C and see whether the spelling B–D–F fits.
claims: Roman numerals represent scale-degree chords independent of key.
Uppercase numerals mean major and lowercase numerals mean minor.
Major-key numerals are I ii iii IV V vi vii°.
In C major, IV = F, V = G and vi = Am.

items.q: What does a lowercase ii tell you?
options: The chord is a seventh chord
items.why: A lowercase numeral marks a minor chord.
misconceptions: The case of a numeral shows dynamics
The case shows repetition
The case shows added notes

items.q: In C major, which chord is V?
items.why: G is the 5th degree of C, and V is uppercase, so the chord is major.
misconceptions: Miscounting degrees lands on the 4th
The V chord is minor
Counting the root as zero lands one degree too high

items.q: Which numeral sequence is correct for a major key?
options: I ii iii IV V vi vii°
I II III IV V VI VII
i ii iii iv v vi vii
I ii III IV v vi vii°
items.answer: I ii iii IV V vi vii°
items.why: This matches the qualities major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished.
misconceptions: Every chord in a key is major
Every chord in a key is minor
The iii and V qualities are reversed

items.q: Why use Roman numerals instead of letter names?
options: The same numbers work in any key
Letter names only work on piano
They show which frets to use
items.answer: The same numbers work in any key
items.why: Numerals name scale degrees, not specific notes.
misconceptions: Numerals affect playing technique
Letter names are tied to one instrument
Numerals are a kind of tablature

items.q: In C major, write I–vi–IV–V as chord names.
items.why: In C, I = C, vi = Am, IV = F and V = G.

items.q: Why is iii written in lowercase?
items.answer: Because the chord on the third degree of a major key is minor.
items.why: Lowercase numerals mean minor chords.

lessons.title: Finding the Chords of Any Key
lessons.objective: Find the seven chords of guitar-friendly keys like G and D, and move a progression between keys.
lessons.hook: G and D are the keys open chords love, so this is where most of your songs will live.
lessons.explain: To find a key's chords, apply I ii iii IV V vi vii° to that key's major scale. The G major scale is G A B C D E F#. G major's chords are G, Am, Bm, C, D, Em, F#°. The D major scale is D E F# G A B C#. D major's chords are D, Em, F#m, G, A, Bm, C#°. The same numeral progression in a new key keeps its sound but shifts its pitch. Example: I–IV–V is C–F–G in C, G–C–D in G and D–G–A in D.
key_facts: To find a key's chords, apply I ii iii IV V vi vii° to that key's major scale.
G major's chords are G, Am, Bm, C, D, Em, F#°.
D major's chords are D, Em, F#m, G, A, Bm, C#°.
The same numeral progression in a new key keeps its sound but shifts its pitch.

predict.q: Is the ii chord in G major A minor, A major or something else?

angles: Lay the C major chord list along a ruler. Slide the whole ruler so it starts on a new note, and every gap stays the same size. Try sliding it to start on A and write what you get.
Build one key from scratch. Write its scale, then place the quality pattern under it like labels. Do this for E major and check each chord on guitar.

rungs.text: A major scale: A B C# D E F# G#. Apply the numerals: I = A, ii = Bm, iii = C#m, IV = D, V = E, vi = F#m, vii° = G#°.
E major scale: E F# G# A B C# D#. I = E, ii = __, iii = G#m, IV = __, V = B, vi = __, vii° = D#°.
Write the seven chords of F major. Its scale is F G A Bb C D E.

claims: A key's chords come from applying the major-key numeral pattern to its scale.
G major's chords are G Am Bm C D Em F#°.
D major's chords are D Em F#m G A Bm C#°.
Transposing a progression keeps its numerals and shifts its pitch.

items.q: What is the V chord in G major?
items.why: D is the 5th note of G major, and V is major.
misconceptions: IV and V are confused
The V chord is minor
V was taken from the key of D

items.q: What is the vi chord in D major?
items.why: B is the 6th degree of D major, and vi is minor.
misconceptions: The vi chord is major
vi was carried over from C major
iii and vi are confused

items.q: I–IV–V in C is C–F–G. What is it in G?
items.why: The numerals stay the same, so you take the I, IV and V chords of G.
misconceptions: This uses the chords of D instead of G
Transposing changes the chord qualities
The numerals were counted as neighboring degrees

items.q: How do you find the chords of a new key?
options: Apply the numeral pattern to its scale
Move all C chords up one fret
Make every chord in it minor
Use only the open chords you know
items.answer: Apply the numeral pattern to its scale
items.why: Every major key uses the same numeral pattern built on its own scale.
misconceptions: Any key is one fret away from C
New keys change the chord qualities
Keys are defined by which chords are easy to play

items.q: Which chord is iii in D major?
items.why: F# is the 3rd degree of D major, and iii is minor.

items.q: Write I–V–vi–IV in G major.
items.why: In G, I = G, V = D, vi = Em and IV = C.

lessons.title: Tonic, Predominant and Dominant
lessons.objective: Group a key's chords by function and predict which chords create tension or rest.
lessons.hook: Function explains why some chord changes feel like arriving home and others feel like a question.
lessons.explain: Chords group into three functions: tonic, predominant, and dominant. Tonic chords (I, and often vi) feel like home. Predominant chords (IV and ii) lead away from home toward the dominant. Dominant chords (V and vii°) create tension that pulls back to I. Example in C: strum C–F–G and stop, and the progression feels unfinished. Add C, and G resolving to C sounds like arriving home.
key_facts: Chords group into three functions: tonic, predominant, and dominant.
Tonic chords (I, and often vi) feel like home.
Predominant chords (IV and ii) lead away from home toward the dominant.
Dominant chords (V and vii°) create tension that pulls back to I.

predict.q: Strum C–F–G and stop. How does it feel?
options: Unfinished, as if it wants to go on
No different from stopping on C
Simply wrong or out of key

angles: Think of a trip: being at home, setting out on the road, then standing at your front door on the way back. In the key of D, play each chord and decide by ear which stage of the trip it feels like.
Play a loop in A major and stop on a different chord each time. Notice which stopping points feel like an ending and which leave you hanging, then match them to their numerals.
claims: Chords can be grouped as tonic, predominant and dominant.
I and often vi have tonic function.
IV and ii have predominant function.
V and vii° have dominant function and pull to I.

items.q: Which chord most strongly pulls toward I?
items.why: V is the dominant, which creates tension that resolves to I.
misconceptions: The predominant pulls hardest to I
vi is the main tension chord
iii is the dominant

items.q: In G major, which chords are predominant?
items.why: IV and ii in G are C and Am.
misconceptions: Dominant chords are predominant

lessons.title: Writing Your First Progressions
lessons.objective: Write four-chord progressions in any key using the tonic, predominant, dominant order and common variations.
lessons.hook: This is the payoff: turning theory into your own chord progressions.
lessons.explain: A strong basic progression moves tonic → predominant → dominant → tonic. I–IV–V–I and I–ii–V–I follow that order. Example in G: G–C–D–G. Swapping I for vi gives a darker start while keeping tonic function, so vi–IV–V–I in G becomes Em–C–D–G. Loops like I–V–vi–IV break the order but still work because they return to I. In C, that loop is C–G–Am–F, and repeating it brings you back to C.
